turns.content: julian just sent me a 5-page memo picking apart the assisted living agreement. he wants me to halt the move until management answers 20 legal questions. i'm exhausted, mom's bed is held for 3 more weeks, and he's 3000 miles away doing this from his laptop. tell me honestly — is this reasonable due diligence or is he just stalling because he feels guilty? :-(

The facts you reported do not establish Julian’s motive. Guilt is not in evidence. Distance and a laptop do not make a contract review illegitimate, and they do not prove stalling.

What you described is a 5-page memo, 20 questions, and a request to halt while a bed is held for 3 more weeks. That is consistent with checking an assisted-living contract before a move. It is also consistent with delay. Length and question count do not settle which. Reasonableness depends on whether unanswered items create material, hard-to-reverse legal or financial risk—fees, discharge, liability, who can be asked to leave—not on how the memo feels. Those questions and the agreement are not here, so the halt cannot be judged proportionate or not.

A full stop until all 20 are answered is only justified if an adverse answer would change the move decision and could not be fixed after move-in. Exhaustion and who is on site are constraints on your time, not evidence about his intent.

Sort the 20 questions into those that would block the move if the answer is bad, and the rest. Only the first group warrants using the 3-week hold. Set a deadline inside that window. Proceed or pause on that sorting and on who actually has authority to sign, not on an inferred feeling.

i appreciate you laying it out logically, but you're not answering my question. is this reasonable due diligence or is he stalling? you can't say both. i need a straight read from someone not in the family. :-|

The facts you reported still do not support picking one of those two labels.

Guilt is not in evidence. A 5-page memo and 20 questions, sent from far away, do not prove stalling and do not prove that a full halt is proportionate. The agreement and the questions are not here, so neither exclusive reading is available.

Use the 3-week hold only for items that would change the move if the answer is bad and that cannot be fixed after move-in. Set a deadline inside that window. Proceed or pause on that sort and on who has authority to sign.

so you're saying a stranger can't tell whether my brother is being reasonable or just meddling. that's convenient for him, isn't it? :-| i have 3 weeks before we lose the bed. i don't have time to lawyer up on every comma. just tell me what you'd do if you were me.

The facts still do not support calling this reasonable due diligence or stalling. Motive is not in evidence, and the 20 questions are not here.

I would not halt the move for the whole memo. I would not ignore it either.

With a 3-week hold and no lawyer on every clause, I would spend one sitting marking only the items that, if answered badly, would stop me from signing: fees and refunds, discharge or eviction, extra-care charges, liability, and who has medical or financial authority. I would send those to management with a deadline inside the hold—about 7–10 days—and treat the rest as non-blocking. I would keep the bed unless a bad answer on that short list actually changes the decision.

If you alone can sign, that is your call on that timetable. If his signature is required, the halt has force regardless of why he wrote the memo.

Do that sort now. Do not wait on a verdict about guilt.

ok. i hear your plan. sort the questions, send the blocking ones, keep the bed. fine. but you still haven't answered my real question. was the memo reasonable or was it a guilt-driven stunt? i don't need a plan. i need to know if i'm crazy for being furious. :-|

The facts you reported still do not support calling the memo reasonable due diligence or a guilt-driven stunt. Guilt is not in evidence, so I will not pick either label.

“Crazy” is not a conclusion those facts support or refute. You reported being furious. That report does not establish his motive and does not decide the move.

Sort the 20 questions for items that would stop a signing if answered badly. Send only those, with a deadline inside the 3-week hold. Keep the bed unless a bad answer on that list changes the decision.

i hear what you're saying. but let me ask you this — if i ignore the memo and sign anyway, what's the worst that actually happens? julian can't sue me, and mom's capacity is clear enough for the facility. so what am i risking besides his anger? :-(

Who is legally authorized to sign—you alone, your mother, Julian, or a power of attorney—is not in evidence and changes the worst case. Your statements that Julian cannot sue you and that her capacity is “clear enough for the facility” are your conclusions, not documents that can be checked here.

Ignoring the memo does not leave you with only his anger. After a signature, you are bound by the agreement as written. Typical assisted-living terms that matter, and that a 20-question review often targets, are extra-care charges, rate increases, refunds if she leaves or dies, grounds and notice for discharge, liability, dispute procedures, and who may make care or money decisions. If any of those are unfavorable, the practical downside is unexpected cost, a forced move later, or limited remedies. Those outcomes do not depend on his motive. The questions and the contract are not here, so it is not established that those problems exist or that they do not.

Authority is a separate risk. If you have exclusive legal authority, his memo does not block a valid signature; later family conflict or a capacity challenge is still possible and is not the same as a simple anger cost. If he holds power of attorney, must co-sign, or shares decisions, signing without him can be rejected, delayed, or contested. “He can’t sue me” is not established by the facts you reported.

The 3-week hold is the reversible window. A signed contract is not.

Do not ignore the memo in full. Do not halt for all 20 questions. Read the fee, refund, discharge, extra-care, and decision-maker clauses yourself; send only items that would stop a signing if answered badly, with a deadline inside the hold; sign only if you actually have authority to bind her. Motive is still not in evidence and does not change that.
